title: manuscript-guard results fragment
description: One analysis script's contribution to the project's results. Machine-written only. A project may contain many fragments; they are merged, and a key defined twice is an error rather than a last-one-wins.

values.description: Flat dotted keys. Nesting is deliberately not supported: a flat namespace makes a key in prose and a key in code the same string.

tables.description: Tables emitted by the analysis and referenced as {{table.<key>}}. Cells are strings already in their display form, for the same reason values carry `display`: the rounding is decided once, where the number was computed.

variables.description: The variables the analysis declares with `variable()`, each with the kind it is meant to be. The data cannot say whether 1 to 4 is a grade, a code or a count; G15 compares the kind with how every model entered the variable, and with what the data were observed to hold.

models.description: The models the analysis fitted, recorded with `model()` as the fit describes itself: engine, formula, terms and how each variable entered them, rows used and dropped, events, convergence. Facts only: the name a model goes by, its generated description and its table are derived when the results are read.

steps.description: The steps of the analysis that ran, each marked in the code with `step()` and pointed at from the Methods by {{method.<name>}}. Each records where its code is and a digest of that code with comments and layout left out, and of the functions of the script it calls. G9 compares the digest with the one recorded when a person last read the step against the Methods text that points at it.

code_lists.description: The code lists the analysis selected on, keyed by the table that prints them. RECORD 6.1 requires these to be published; keeping them as data beside the rendered table means the paper prints the list the code actually used, and the next study can reuse the definition rather than retyping it.

lines.description: The first and last line of the step's code in the script, where the emitter could read them.

follows.description: The functions the step calls that are defined in the analysis itself, whose code the digest covers too. A function from a package is not followed.

composed.description: Which cells the emitter built from numbers rather than receiving as text, and what it built them from. A composed cell and a typed one are the same characters by the time anyone reads this file, so without this record the rule that every number in a table was published by the analysis can only be enforced inside the emitter that wrote it — which makes it a rule an author steps around by switching language. With it, G2 applies the same rule to any fragment.

row.description: Index into `rows`. Omitted for a column header.

template.description: The emitter's template, with `{}` where each part went. The gate rebuilds the cell from this and `parts` and requires the result to equal the text on the page, so a claim of composition has to describe the cell it is attached to. The template's own wording is then checked like any other text: `"{} (n = 412)"` would otherwise smuggle a count in under the exemption.

codes.description: This cell is a join of the code list published under `code_lists` for the same table and row, and is checked against it. A code list carries no number the emitter derived, so rebuilding it from a declared part would prove nothing - the part would be the text.

parts.description: The displays the emitter derived for this cell, in template order. They excuse the numbers in *this* cell and nowhere else: folded into one project-wide set, a single entry anywhere - even in a table with no rows - whitelisted its strings everywhere.

value.description: The machine value. Comparisons and figures use this.

display.description: Exactly how the value is written in prose. Set at emit time so the same quantity cannot be rounded two different ways in two places; this is what makes cross-artefact consistency free rather than checked.

digits.description: Decimal places, used to derive `display` when it is not given. A float with neither `display` nor `digits` is rejected: leaving the rounding implicit is how two sections come to disagree.

quoted.description: Whether this value is expected to appear in a deliverable. Set false to declare an intermediate deliberately, which exempts it from coverage checking. Coverage exists to catch values silently dropped from the manuscript, so opting out must be explicit.

label.description: This string value is a name or a period, not a measurement. A string value is its own display and nothing checked what was inside it, so `em.value("ror.headline", "12.34 (95% CI 8.00 to 19.00)")` published a fabricated estimate and interval through an ordinary binding. Digit-bearing strings are still wanted - a genotype, a study period - so this is an opt-in rather than a ban.

bounds.description: The key of the estimate this value is a bound of. Written by `interval()`. Three keys named point, ci_low and ci_high are three unrelated numbers to every check, so a manuscript could quote the upper bound where the lower belongs and every binding would still resolve.

bound.description: Which end of the interval. With `bounds`, this is what lets G2 read the order the bounds are quoted in and refuse an interval printed backwards.

level.description: Which interval this bound belongs to, when one estimate carries more than one - "90%" beside a 95% CI, or "95% CrI" beside a frequentist one. Bounds are compared within a level and never across: a 90% interval nested inside a 95% one is correct, not a contradiction. Absent means the estimate's only interval.

role.description: What the value is, when it is neither a measurement nor a label. `parameter` is a choice the analysis made and used (`em.parameter`), `software` the version of a piece of software the run imported (`em.software`). G2 fails one of these typed in the text where it should be bound, because a threshold typed in the Methods passes as a convention and stays one after the code has changed.

read.description: For a parameter: whether the script reads again the value `parameter()` handed back, as the emitter found by reading the script where the call stands. False when the value is thrown away or assigned to a name nothing reads, which G2 fails; absent when the emitter could not tell. A read is not proof that the value changes a result.

same_as.description: Another key this value is the same quantity as. G8 notices two keys holding the same number and goes quiet the moment they diverge, which is when it matters; nothing else in this file records that two keys were meant to agree. A declaration rather than an inference, because the question is about intent: ror.point, ror.ci_low and ror.ci_high share everything a heuristic could see and are supposed to differ.

label.description: How the paper names the variable.

observed.description: What the data held of the variable when the analysis ran.

name.description: What the paper calls the model.

description.description: What the model is for, in the author's words. No fit can say.

engine.description: What the fit says of itself: language, package, class, family and link.

events.description: For a binary outcome: the rows where it occurred.

events_by_level.description: For a binary outcome: events at each level of each categorical term.

generated_by.description: Project-relative path of the script that wrote this fragment.

generated_by_sha256.description: Digest of that script as it stood when it wrote this fragment. G1 compares it rather than modification times, because an mtime is set by `touch`: editing the analysis and stamping the fragment forward used to hide the change entirely. Optional, so a fragment written before this field existed still validates; G1 falls back to the mtime comparison for those.

inputs.description: Every data file read. Hashes are what let the freshness gate notice that data changed even when nothing was touched afterwards.

session.description: Enough of the computing environment to reconstruct it.
